extracted.intended_audience: general readers; educators; journalists; researchers interested in plagiarism/Wikipedia
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia list-article documenting notable instances where individuals or institutions copied material from Wikipedia without proper attribution, and summarizing the licensing/attribution requirement and consequences. Useful as a descriptive resource about plagiarism cases, not a how-to or policy guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative Commons attribution requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors to the online encyclopedia Wikipedia license their submitted content under a Creative Commons license, which permits re-use as long as attribution is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to give the necessary attribution when re-using Wikipedia content is a violation of the Creative Commons license. The page repeatedly emphasizes that re-use is permitted only with proper attribution; examples and citations illustrate when attribution was omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism defined as passing off Wikipedia content as one’s own
rubrics_metrics.description: There have been a number of occasions when persons have failed to give the necessary attribution and attempted to pass off material from Wikipedia as their own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats such unattributed copying as plagiarism — an ethical and legal wrongdoing. Examples include copying large passages verbatim into books, theses, government documents, reports, and political materials. The entry lists many notable individuals and institutions credibly accused of this behavior (e.g., authors, politicians, publishers, government bodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic/educational copying is treated as plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: In educational settings, students sometimes copy Wikipedia to fulfill class assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites a Turnitin study (2011) finding Wikipedia among the most-copied websites by secondary and higher-education students, implying that such copying constitutes academic dishonesty and may trigger institutional responses. The page also gives examples of exam/marking guides and theses where unattributed copying occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of unattributed copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism from Wikipedia, when discovered, can be a reason for embarrassment, professional sanctions, or legal issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents concrete outcomes in many cases: book retractions (e.g., Elsevier 2020 retraction), public apologies, investigative media exposure, institutional investigations, and reputational damage. These examples serve as practical warnings about consequences for failing to attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antipatterns: wholesale copying and failure to paraphrase or cite
rubrics_metrics.description: Large sections copied wholesale from unattributed websites (including Wikipedia) are repeatedly cited as problematic practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several incidents described involve copying 'large sections copied wholesale' into marking guides, books, reports, or speeches. The article implicitly discourages verbatim copying without citation and highlights cases where close paraphrasing without attribution was treated as plagiarism.
